questions.questionText: What property makes embeddings useful, that a raw token ID doesn't have?
options: Embeddings are always smaller numbers than token IDs
Semantically similar tokens end up close together in the vector space, so distance/similarity reflects meaning
Embeddings remove the need for tokenization
Embeddings are only used for images, not text
questions.correctAnswer: Semantically similar tokens end up close together in the vector space, so distance/similarity reflects meaning
questions.explanation: A raw token ID is an arbitrary index with no inherent relationship to other IDs; embeddings are learned specifically so that geometric closeness corresponds to semantic closeness.

questions.questionText: Where does an embedding's "similar words end up close together" property actually come from?
options: It's manually programmed by engineers for each word
It emerges from training a model to predict context (nearby or masked words) across huge amounts of text — words in similar contexts end up with similar vectors
It's a random accident with no underlying cause
It only happens for the 100 most common English words
questions.correctAnswer: It emerges from training a model to predict context (nearby or masked words) across huge amounts of text — words in similar contexts end up with similar vectors
questions.explanation: This clustering behavior is a side effect of the training objective, not something explicitly designed in — words that appear in similar contexts get pushed toward similar vectors purely through gradient descent on that objective.

questions.questionText: What does cosine similarity measure between two embedding vectors?
options: The exact Euclidean distance between them
The cosine of the angle between them, largely ignoring vector magnitude, ranging from -1 to 1
The number of dimensions they share
Whether the two vectors have the same length
questions.correctAnswer: The cosine of the angle between them, largely ignoring vector magnitude, ranging from -1 to 1
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity focuses on direction rather than magnitude, which is the standard way to compare embedding vectors for semantic similarity.
